title: Microsoft Unveils Maia 300, Plans Multi-Gigawatt Rollout of Its Own AI Chips From 2027
excerpt: Maia will become the primary inference system for Copilot, Teams and GitHub, as Microsoft moves to cut the cost of running AI on Nvidia hardware. Nadella called it the company's biggest bet yet on its own silicon.
body:
• Microsoft unveiled Maia 300, its third-generation AI accelerator, and said it will scale the Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027.
  • Maia will become the primary inference system for Microsoft's own products — Copilot, Teams, GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry — a direct bid to cut the cost of running AI at scale.
  • Microsoft claims Maia 300 delivers 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems; the figures are the company's own and not independently verified.
  • Maia 200 is already in production across the US, Europe and Australia; Microsoft says it will keep buying Nvidia and AMD chips alongside its own.

Microsoft is making its largest bet yet on its own silicon. The company on Monday unveiled Maia 300, the third generation of its Azure AI accelerator, and announced plans to expand the Maia system to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027 — making its home-grown chips, rather than Nvidia's GPUs, the primary engine running Microsoft's AI products.

Chief Executive Satya Nadella called the announcement "our biggest bet yet on our own silicon." Scott Guthrie, executive vice president for cloud and AI, set out the plan on the official Microsoft blog: Maia becomes the primary inference system for Microsoft products and services, the machinery that answers when a user prompts Copilot, joins a Teams meeting or accepts a GitHub suggestion.

The numbers Microsoft is claiming

Maia 300 is built for inference — long-context reasoning, fast conversational responses and multi-step agentic workloads. Microsoft says a full rack of 96 accelerators delivers up to seven times the token throughput of a Maia 200 rack, and about 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems. Each chip carries eight stacks of HBM4 memory totalling 288 GB, with 18 terabytes per second of bandwidth, and is manufactured by TSMC on its N2P process. These are Microsoft's own figures, published without an identified comparison system, and they have not been independently benchmarked.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=8W2agm_nmjo

"We are confident we have built the best product for these workloads. We are backing that confidence by deploying Maia at gigawatt scale starting next year."

— Rani Borkar, President, Azure Hardware Systems and Infrastructure

Maia 200 is already working

The announcement is an escalation of something already running, not a paper launch. Maia 200 is in production across data centres in the United States, Europe and Australia, serving Microsoft Copilot and running OpenAI models, Microsoft's own MAI models and open-source models. Microsoft says it delivers up to 1.7 times more tokens per watt than leading GPU infrastructure for built-in AI features in Teams, Copilot and Cowork. GitHub Copilot and Microsoft Foundry workloads are due to move onto it by the end of this year.

Why it matters beyond Microsoft

Reuters framed the push around cost: inference is now the dominant expense of the AI business, and every token Microsoft serves on its own chips is a token it does not rent from Nvidia's margins. Microsoft was explicit that it will keep buying Nvidia and AMD processors — this is a shift in the centre of gravity, not a divorce. For the wider industry, including the Indian IT services firms that build on Azure, a cheaper inference stack changes the economics of every AI product layered on top of it. The detailed technical report is due at Ignite in November; production deployments of Maia 300 begin in 2027.
